## Why the Sky Is Blue

Sunlight contains all the colors of the visible spectrum, but when it enters Earth's atmosphere it collides with gas molecules (primarily nitrogen and oxygen) that are much smaller than the wavelength of light. These tiny particles scatter the incoming light in all directions, and they scatter shorter wavelengths far more effectively than longer ones. As a result, the blue and violet portions of sunlight are redistributed across the sky, reaching our eyes from every direction and giving the daytime sky its characteristic blue color. (The sky appears blue rather than violet because the Sun emits less violet light, some violet is absorbed higher in the atmosphere, and the human eye is simply more sensitive to blue than to violet.)

## Rayleigh Scattering Wavelength Dependence

The intensity of light scattered by small particles is inversely proportional to the **fourth power of the wavelength**:

$$I \propto \frac{1}{\lambda^4}$$

This strong dependence explains why blue light (~450 nm) scatters roughly ten times more than red light (~700 nm), since $\left(\frac{700}{450}\right)^4 \approx 10$.

I ∝ 1/λ⁴

So the full statement: I_scattered ∝ 1/λ⁴
